Apple has filed a proposal regarding the fees it is permitted to charge for transactions conducted outside the App Store system in the Epic Games case. Details below.

Apple Files Proposal for Commissions Outside the App Store

After several attempts to stay the district court proceedings—which will determine how much, if anything, Apple can charge for transactions made outside the App Store's IAP system—Apple has now filed a statement setting out its proposed fee structure.

Apple's filing of the statement coincides with the Supreme Court denying its application to stay the lower court proceedings while the case is under review. The Supreme Court is examining whether Apple can be held in contempt, after the company continued to charge a 27% commission on transactions outside the App Store despite an injunction issued by Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods.

Apple had argued before the lower court, and subsequently before the Supreme Court, that the Supreme Court's ruling could affect the outcome of the fee determination proceedings, and therefore those proceedings should be stayed until the Supreme Court issues its decision. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's application, allowing the lower court proceedings to continue during the review.

As a result, Apple has now submitted its proposal, which recommends:

Standard apps would be charged 15%, compared with the current 30% in-app purchase ("IAP") commission; the Video Partner Program ("VPP"), News Partner Program ("NPP"), Mini Apps Partner Program ("MPP"), and subscription renewals would be charged 10%; apps under the Small Business Program would be charged 5%.

Apple stated that "factual and expert evidence regarding these proposed commission rates has been submitted concurrently." The company added:

Apple also noted that its "proposed outlinks commission could be benchmarked against commissions charged by other app stores that compete with the App Store," including Google Play, the Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also noted that "Google Play Store charges a 'standard' rate of 20%, a programme rate of 15%, and a subscription rate of 10% for outlinks—rates which Epic has also agreed to."

Apple said it still believes the fee determination proceedings should be stayed during the Supreme Court's review of the case, adding that the submission of the proposal was solely to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also pointed out that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's ruling that imposed a blanket ban on commissions for outlink transactions, noting that commissions are only problematic when they effectively amount to a prohibitive effect.

Following the submission of the statement, Epic will now have an opportunity to respond, and Apple is expected to file its submissions with the Supreme Court by 14 September.
